q480: After a frightening event, the brain sometimes stores the memory in a raw, unprocessed way, with all the sights, sounds and body sensations still vivid. This is why a flashback can feel like it is happening now, not then. The amygdala, the brain's alarm, links sounds like screeching brakes with danger and fires instantly. Research suggests that the part of the brain that labels memories with time and place may work less well during intense fear. When flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance and jumpiness last longer than a month, it may be post-traumatic stress, which is a treatable condition. Anita's guilt was also adding to her distress.
q481: A senior doctor at her hospital noticed her trembling at a siren and gently asked if she was okay. Anita broke down. The doctor referred her to a trauma-trained therapist. Hearing that her reactions were a normal response to an abnormal event, and that help existed, gave her hope.
q482: Began trauma-focused therapy, including EMDR, with a qualified therapist
q483: Used 5-4-3-2-1 grounding during flashbacks to remind herself she was safe now
q484: Practised orienting by looking around the room slowly and naming the date
q485: Used the container exercise to set aside memories between therapy sessions
q486: Built a safe place image where she sensed Jesus with her
q487: Returned to riding slowly, first in an empty ground with her brother
q488: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore will not we fear (Psalm 46:1-2). The psalms are full of people who were attacked, afraid and shaken, and who cried out honestly. When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee (Isaiah 43:2). God does not promise we will never face terror, but that He will be present in it. Jesus Himself suffered trauma on the cross, and He understands our pain. Getting therapy was not a lack of faith. Luke was a physician, and God often heals through skilled helpers. Anita learned that God was with her on that road, and He was with her in her healing too.
q489: God designed the brain to process difficult memories over time. Usually this happens naturally, especially during sleep. But sometimes a memory gets stuck. Therapies like EMDR and trauma-focused cognitive therapy, in studies, help many people process stuck memories so they feel more like past events and less like present danger. Grounding brings the thinking brain back online by focusing on the present. Orienting to the room tells the alarm system there is no threat here and now. The brain's ability to change means that a stuck memory can be gently updated, so the past stays in the past.
q490: Psalm 46:1|God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
q494: After four months of therapy, Anita's flashbacks were much less frequent and less intense. Sudden screeches still make her jump, and around the accident anniversary her nightmares returned for a few nights. But she now rides her scooter short distances in daylight. She has started telling other nurses that trauma therapy works and that needing help is not weakness.
q495: Traumatic memories can heal with time, skilled help and the steady presence of God.
q496: After something scary, our brain can keep remembering it as if it is happening again. Kind helpers and God help our brain know we are safe now.
q497: Meera and the silent prayer room
q498: Meera, 38, a schoolteacher and worship leader in Kochi
q499: For eleven years Meera had led worship at her church in Kochi. She loved it. But after a hard year, with her father's long illness, extra classes at school and two children preparing for board exams, something went quiet inside her. She still sang on Sundays. She still opened her Bible each morning. But the words felt like cardboard. When she prayed, it was like talking into an empty room. She began to wonder whether God had stepped away, or whether she had done something wrong. She felt like a fraud standing on the stage with her eyes closed while people around her wept. One evening she told her husband, quietly, that she might stop leading. 'I cannot give what I do not have,' she said, and then she cried for a long time.
q500: Meera was not faithless. She was exhausted. After a long season of caring and pushing through, the nervous system can slide into a low, flat state. Research suggests that chronic stress can dull the brain's reward and feeling systems, so even good things feel muted. This is sometimes called hypoarousal or shutdown. Her body was protecting her by turning the volume down. Underneath, there was also unspoken grief about her father that she had never let herself feel. And she held a quiet belief from childhood: God is close when I feel Him, and far when I do not. So numbness felt like proof that she had been abandoned, when it was really a tired body and a heart carrying sorrow.
q501: Her pastor's wife listened without fixing anything. Then she said, 'Meera, maybe God is not asking you to perform right now. Maybe He is inviting you to rest and to be honest.' Meera realised she had been treating prayer as another duty to get right. She gave herself permission to stop pretending and to bring God her real, tired heart.
q502: Took a three-week break from leading worship, with her pastor's blessing
q503: Prayed a short breath prayer morning and night instead of long sessions
q504: Sat quietly for five minutes on the terrace, simply being with God
q505: Wrote a lament about her father's illness and read it aloud to God
q506: Noticed and wrote down three small glimmers of goodness each day
q507: Saw her doctor, who checked her iron and thyroid and found low iron
q508: The Bible is full of people who felt God was far away. David cried, 'How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD?' (Psalm 13:1). Elijah, burnt out under a juniper tree, did not receive a lecture. God gave him sleep, food, and then a still small voice (1 Kings 19:5-12). Jesus Himself prayed, 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Matthew 27:46). Feeling far from God is not the same as being far from Him. God promises, 'I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee' (Hebrews 13:5). Lament is not a lack of faith. It is faith that keeps talking to God even when He feels silent. Rest is not laziness either. It is trust that God holds things while we sleep.
q509: God made us as whole people, not floating spirits. Our body, emotions and spirit are woven together, so a drained body can make the soul feel dry. When we rest, eat well and allow grief to move, the nervous system slowly comes out of shutdown and feeling returns. God also built us for connection. Being heard by a kind friend calms the stress system in a way that trying harder alone cannot. Simple, repeated practices like breath prayer give the brain a gentle rhythm of safety. Over time the heart becomes able to sense God's nearness again.
q510: Psalm 34:18|The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart
q514: There was no dramatic moment. After about two months, Meera noticed she was humming a hymn while cooking, and it meant something again. Some mornings still felt flat, and that scared her at first. She learned to say, 'This is a dry day, not a lost faith.' Iron tablets helped her energy. She returned to leading worship once a month instead of every week, and she now tells her team that honesty is welcome.
q515: A season of feeling far from God is often a call to rest and honest lament, not a sign that He has left.
q516: Sometimes we feel far from God because we are very tired. God stays close even when we cannot feel Him.
q517: Arjun and the prayer that went unanswered
q518: Arjun, 29, a software tester in Pune whose mother died of cancer
q519: Arjun prayed for his mother every day for fourteen months. His whole prayer group fasted. A visiting preacher had even said she would be healed. Then, on a rainy night in July, she died in a hospital in Pune. At the funeral, people said, 'She is in a better place,' and Arjun nodded. Inside, something cracked. He stopped reading his Bible. When friends sent verses on WhatsApp, he muted the chat. He began to think, 'Either God could not heal her, or He did not care enough to.' He still went to church for his father's sake, but he sat at the back with his arms folded. He felt guilty for doubting and angry at the guilt. Late at night he searched online for reasons faith might not be true.
q520: Arjun was carrying grief and confusion at the same time. When a deep hope collapses, the brain experiences it as a kind of injury. The pain of loss and the shock of a broken expectation stack on top of each other. Underneath was a hidden belief he had absorbed: if I pray with enough faith, God must do what I ask. When that formula failed, his whole picture of God seemed to fall with it. He also had no safe place to say his doubts aloud, because his church culture treated questions as weakness. Unspoken grief often turns into numbness or anger. His folded arms were protecting a heart that felt betrayed.
q521: A friend from college, who had lost her own brother, said, 'You are allowed to be angry with God. He can take it.' She showed him how much of the Psalms is people arguing with God. For the first time, Arjun prayed honestly: 'I am angry with You. I do not understand.' It was the first real prayer in months.
q522: Wrote a raw lament to God about his mother and kept it in his notes app
q523: Met monthly with an older believer who welcomed his questions
q524: Joined a grief support group run by a local counsellor
q525: Read the book of Job slowly, one chapter a week
q526: Allowed himself to cry when he passed the hospital, instead of pushing it down
q527: Scripture never pretends that every prayer is answered the way we hope. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed, and God said, 'My grace is sufficient for thee' (2 Corinthians 12:9). Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, 'Let this cup pass from me,' and the cup did not pass (Matthew 26:39). Job asked hard questions for many chapters, and God called his honest words more right than his friends' tidy answers (Job 42:7). God does not promise to explain every loss, but He promises to be present in it. 'Jesus wept' (John 11:35), even knowing He would raise Lazarus. Grief and faith can sit in the same heart.
q528: God designed us to process pain through expression and connection. Research suggests that putting feelings into words calms the brain's alarm system and helps the thinking brain make sense of what happened. Grief that is spoken and shared slowly loosens its grip, while grief that is hidden tends to stay frozen or come out as anger. We are also made to borrow strength from others. Sitting with someone who has suffered helps our nervous system feel less alone. Faith that has room for questions becomes deeper and more honest, not weaker.
q529: Psalm 62:8|Trust in him at all times, ye people, pour out your heart before him
q533: Arjun still does not know why his mother died. Some Sundays he still feels angry. But he has stopped searching for reasons to leave and started bringing his questions to God directly. On the first anniversary of her death he went to her grave with his father, and they prayed together for the first time since the funeral. He says his faith is smaller in certainty but bigger in honesty.
q534: God welcomes honest questions and grief, and faith can survive an unanswered prayer when it has room to lament.
q535: When God does not answer the way we want, we can still tell Him how sad and angry we feel. He listens and stays with us.
q536: Priya and the father who never said sorry
q537: Priya, 34, a nurse in Hyderabad, married with one daughter
q538: Priya's father drank when she was a child. He was never violent with her, but he shouted, broke things and once forgot to pick her up from school until nine at night. Now he was sober, older and wanted to be close to his granddaughter. Everyone at home said, 'That was long ago. He has changed. Forgive and forget.' Priya tried. She smiled at family functions. But whenever he held her daughter, her chest tightened and she felt a hot wave of anger. Then she felt guilty, because she was a Christian and was supposed to forgive. At church, a sermon on forgiveness left her in tears in the car park. She told her husband, 'I keep forgiving him, and the anger keeps coming back. Maybe I am not really saved.'
q539: Priya was confusing forgiveness with forgetting and with instant trust. Her body still remembered the nights of fear. Research on trauma suggests that early frightening experiences are stored as body memories, so a tight chest can fire before any conscious thought. That is not a failure of faith. Her anger was also protecting something precious: the little girl who waited alone at school and was never comforted. No one had ever said to that child, 'What happened to you was wrong.' Because her hurt had never been named and grieved, every attempt to forgive felt like pressing a lid on a boiling pot.
q540: A Christian counsellor told her, 'Forgiveness is not saying it did not matter. It is saying it mattered so much that you are handing it to God.' Priya realised she had never actually let herself say how much it hurt. Forgiveness had to begin with honesty.
q541: Wrote a list of specific hurts instead of a vague 'he was bad'
q542: Wrote an unsent letter to her father describing what she needed as a child
q543: Worked through a forgiveness process in counselling, one hurt at a time
q544: Set a gentle boundary that her father would not drive her daughter alone yet
q545: Used a calming breath when her chest tightened at family events
